questions.stem: In ED, Terry, 20, has severe acute asthma. He can say only 3 to 5 words at a time, so you are keeping the history short. You have started treatment and now want the single question that best tells you whether he is at risk of a fatal attack. Which question should you ask?
options: "Does anyone in your family have asthma, eczema, hayfever or other allergies?"
"How old were you when you were first told you had asthma?"
"Have you ever needed intensive care or a breathing tube for asthma?"
"Do dust, cats or pollen ever set off your wheeze?"
questions.why: A previous ICU admission or intubation is the strongest single marker of risk for a fatal asthma attack. Other markers are hospital admission, systemic steroids, reliever-only use, no preventer and no action plan.
notes: A family history of atopy supports the diagnosis of asthma, but it does not tell you whether this patient is at risk of a fatal attack.
Age at diagnosis does not mark risk of a fatal attack, and it wastes his limited breath.
Knowing his allergen triggers helps prevention later, but it does not grade how dangerous his asthma is.

questions.stem: Terry, 20, arrives in ED with severe acute asthma: he speaks in phrases, uses his accessory muscles, has RR 28 and SpO2 93% on room air. He has no life-threatening features and no cannula yet. He has had 8 puffs of his own salbutamol without a spacer. What is the most appropriate initial bronchodilator regimen?
options: Salbutamol 100 microgram pMDI via spacer, 4 puffs every 4 hours and review after 24 hours
Salbutamol 100 microgram pMDI via spacer, 12 puffs every 20 minutes for the first hour
Salbutamol IV infusion, started before any further inhaled doses
Salbutamol 2.5 mg nebulised once, then reassess in 4 hours
questions.why: For severe acute asthma in an adult, give salbutamol 12 puffs (100 microgram each) via spacer every 20 minutes for the first hour, or 5 mg nebulised every 20 minutes. Add ipratropium, and reassess after each dose.
notes: 4 puffs every 4 hours is a maintenance or mild dose. It is far too little and too infrequent for a severe attack.
IV salbutamol is reserved for life-threatening asthma that is not responding to inhaled treatment, under senior care. It is not first-line.
A single 2.5 mg nebule followed by a 4-hour gap underdoses him. Severe asthma needs 5 mg repeated every 20 minutes.

questions.stem: Terry, 20, has severe acute asthma with widespread wheeze. His SpO2 is 93% on room air and he is breathing at 28 per minute. His spirometry from a few months ago, taken when well, showed a normal TLCO (93% predicted). What is the main mechanism of his hypoxaemia?
options: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch from uneven narrowing of the airways
Impaired gas diffusion across a thickened alveolar-capillary membrane in the lung bases
Alveolar hypoventilation from reduced central respiratory drive
Right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale
questions.why: In acute asthma, uneven bronchoconstriction, mucus and oedema under-ventilate alveoli that are still perfused, so the blood leaving them is poorly oxygenated. This V/Q mismatch usually responds to modest supplemental oxygen.
notes: Asthma affects the airways, not the alveolar membrane. His normal TLCO shows that gas transfer is preserved.
He is tachypnoeic with a high respiratory drive. Hypoventilation only appears late, with exhaustion, as a rising PaCO2.
Nothing suggests an intracardiac shunt, and a true shunt would barely respond to oxygen, whereas his sats improve with it.

questions.stem: Terry, 20, with severe acute asthma, is given ipratropium 8 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes alongside his salbutamol. Ipratropium is a muscarinic antagonist that reduces the cholinergic bronchoconstrictor tone of airway smooth muscle. Which nerve carries the parasympathetic supply to the bronchi?
questions.why: Parasympathetic fibres in the vagus nerve reach the bronchi through the pulmonary plexus. Their acetylcholine acts on M3 receptors to constrict the bronchi and increase mucus secretion, and ipratropium blocks these receptors.
notes: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) is the motor supply to the diaphragm. It does not supply bronchial smooth muscle.
The sympathetic trunk is the autonomic supply that opposes the parasympathetic one. Bronchodilation is mainly driven by circulating adrenaline acting on beta-2 receptors, not by vagal tone.
Intercostal nerves supply the intercostal muscles and the chest wall, not the airway smooth muscle.
